results.name: decade_boundary_effect
results.description: Among non-example targets 1-5 away from their nearest example, yes rate when the target shares that example's tens decade (same value of (x-1)//10) minus when it crosses a decade boundary; observed above null_mean means people treat decades as categories beyond what the model's uniform intervals and rules predict, below means less.
results.code:
# name: decade_boundary_effect
# description: Among non-example targets 1-5 away from their nearest example, yes rate when the target shares that example's tens decade (same value of (x-1)//10) minus when it crosses a decade boundary; observed above null_mean means people treat decades as categories beyond what the model's uniform intervals and rules predict, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    u = df["number_set"].unique()
    ex = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in str(s).split(",")]) for s in u}
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    tab = np.zeros((len(u), 101), dtype=int)
    dist = np.zeros((len(u), 101), dtype=int)
    for i, s in enumerate(u):
        a = np.arange(101)
        dd = np.abs(a[:, None] - ex[s][None, :])
        k = dd.argmin(axis=1)
        tab[i] = ex[s][k]
        dist[i] = dd.min(axis=1)
    idx = pd.Series(range(len(u)), index=u)[df["number_set"]].to_numpy()
    near = tab[idx, t]
    d = dist[idx, t]
    keep = (d >= 1) & (d <= 5)
    same = keep & ((t - 1) // 10 == (near - 1) // 10)
    cross = keep & ~same
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    if same.sum() == 0 or cross.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[same].mean() - r[cross].mean())

results.name: single_example_parity_contrast
results.description: For single-example sets, yes rate on non-example targets with the same parity as the example minus opposite-parity targets; observed above null_mean means people generalize a lone example along odd/even more than the model predicts, below means the model over-weights parity rules for one example.
results.code:
# name: single_example_parity_contrast
# description: For single-example sets, yes rate on non-example targets with the same parity as the example minus opposite-parity targets; observed above null_mean means people generalize a lone example along odd/even more than the model predicts, below means the model over-weights parity rules for one example.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",")
    e = pd.to_numeric(s.where(single, "0")).astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    keep = single & (t != e)
    same = keep & ((t % 2) == (e % 2))
    diff = keep & ((t % 2) != (e % 2))
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    if same.sum() == 0 or diff.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[same].mean() - r[diff].mean())

results.name: near_hull_upward_asymmetry
results.description: For multi-example sets, yes rate on targets 1-15 above the largest example minus targets 1-15 below the smallest example; observed above null_mean means people extend generalization upward (to larger numbers) more than the direction-symmetric model predicts, below means they extend downward more.
results.code:
# name: near_hull_upward_asymmetry
# description: For multi-example sets, yes rate on targets 1-15 above the largest example minus targets 1-15 below the smallest example; observed above null_mean means people extend generalization upward (to larger numbers) more than the direction-symmetric model predicts, below means they extend downward more.
def test_statistic(df):
    u = df["number_set"].unique()
    ex = {s: [int(x) for x in str(s).split(",")] for s in u}
    mx = df["number_set"].map({s: max(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).astype(int)
    mn = df["number_set"].map({s: min(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).astype(int)
    n = df["number_set"].map({s: len(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    up = (n >= 2) & (t > mx) & (t - mx <= 15)
    dn = (n >= 2) & (t < mn) & (mn - t <= 15)
    if up.sum() == 0 or dn.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[up].mean() - r[dn].mean())

results.name: far_target_breadth_drift
results.description: Yes rate on non-example targets more than 20 from every example in the second half of the session (trial_index above median) minus the first half; observed below null_mean means people's distant generalization narrows over the session more than the stationary model predicts, above means it broadens.
results.code:
# name: far_target_breadth_drift
# description: Yes rate on non-example targets more than 20 from every example in the second half of the session (trial_index above median) minus the first half; observed below null_mean means people's distant generalization narrows over the session more than the stationary model predicts, above means it broadens.
def test_statistic(df):
    u = df["number_set"].unique()
    ex = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in str(s).split(",")]) for s in u}
    a = np.arange(101)
    dist = np.stack([np.abs(a[:, None] - ex[s][None, :]).min(axis=1) for s in u])
    idx = pd.Series(range(len(u)), index=u)[df["number_set"]].to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    far = dist[idx, t] > 20
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    late = ti > np.median(ti)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a1 = far & late
    a0 = far & ~late
    if a1.sum() == 0 or a0.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a1].mean() - r[a0].mean())

results.name: small_rule_member_contrast
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples that all fall in some listed rule with at most 12 members (powers of 2/3/4, n^2, squares, cubes, multiples of 10, etc.; smallest such rule used), yes rate on non-example rule-member targets minus non-member targets; observed below null_mean means people generalize less sharply along small mathematical rules than the model (model too all-or-none), above means sharper.
results.code:
# name: small_rule_member_contrast
# description: For sets of 2+ examples that all fall in some listed rule with at most 12 members (powers of 2/3/4, n^2, squares, cubes, multiples of 10, etc.; smallest such rule used), yes rate on non-example rule-member targets minus non-member targets; observed below null_mean means people generalize less sharply along small mathematical rules than the model (model too all-or-none), above means sharper.
def test_statistic(df):
    N = range(1, 101)
    rules = [[2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64], [3, 9, 27, 81], [4, 16, 64], [5, 25], [6, 36], [7, 49], [8, 64], [9, 81], [10, 100],
             [1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100], [1, 8, 27, 64]]
    rules += [[i for i in N if i % n == 0] for n in range(3, 13)]
    rules += [[i for i in N if i % 10 == d] for d in range(1, 10)]
    rules = [set(x) for x in rules if len(x) <= 12]
    best = {}
    for s in df["number_set"].unique():
        e = set(int(x) for x in str(s).split(","))
        if len(e) < 2:
            continue
        c = [x for x in rules if e <= x]
        if c:
            best[s] = min(c, key=len)
    if not best:
        return 0.0
    sub = df[df["number_set"].isin(list(best))]
    t = sub["target"].astype(int)
    mem = pd.Series([tt in best[s] for s, tt in zip(sub["number_set"], t)], index=sub.index)
    isex = pd.Series([str(tt) in str(s).split(",") for s, tt in zip(sub["number_set"], t)], index=sub.index)
    r = sub["rating"].astype(float)
    a = mem & ~isex
    b = ~mem
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: within_set_target_spread
results.description: Mean over sets with at least 5 distinct asked targets of the standard deviation, across targets, of each (set, target) cell's yes rate; observed above null_mean means people's generalization profiles within a set are more sharply contrasted (all-or-none across targets) than the model predicts, below means flatter/more graded.
results.code:
# name: within_set_target_spread
# description: Mean over sets with at least 5 distinct asked targets of the standard deviation, across targets, of each (set, target) cell's yes rate; observed above null_mean means people's generalization profiles within a set are more sharply contrasted (all-or-none across targets) than the model predicts, below means flatter/more graded.
def test_statistic(df):
    cell = df.groupby(["number_set", "target"])["rating"].mean()
    g = cell.groupby(level=0)
    sd = g.std(ddof=0)
    cnt = g.size()
    sd = sd[cnt >= 5]
    if len(sd) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(sd.mean())

results.name: even_set_parity_contrast
results.description: For sets of 2-4 examples that are all even, yes rate on even non-example targets minus odd targets; observed above null_mean means people use the broad "even numbers" rule more than the model predicts, below means the model over-weights parity for even sets.
results.code:
# name: even_set_parity_contrast
# description: For sets of 2-4 examples that are all even, yes rate on even non-example targets minus odd targets; observed above null_mean means people use the broad "even numbers" rule more than the model predicts, below means the model over-weights parity for even sets.
def test_statistic(df):
    u = df["number_set"].unique()
    ok = {s: (lambda e: len(e) >= 2 and all(v % 2 == 0 for v in e))([int(x) for x in str(s).split(",")]) for s in u}
    sel = df["number_set"].map(ok).astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    isex = pd.Series([str(tt) in str(s).split(",") for s, tt in zip(df["number_set"], t)], index=df.index)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    ev = sel & ~isex & (t % 2 == 0)
    od = sel & (t % 2 == 1)
    if ev.sum() == 0 or od.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[ev].mean() - r[od].mean())

results.name: round_target_bias
results.description: For sets whose examples are not all multiples of 10, yes rate on non-example targets that are multiples of 10 minus yes rate on other non-example targets; observed above null_mean means people favour round-number targets beyond what the model's concept posterior predicts (model lacks a round-number bias), below means the model over-endorses them.
results.code:
# name: round_target_bias
# description: For sets whose examples are not all multiples of 10, yes rate on non-example targets that are multiples of 10 minus yes rate on other non-example targets; observed above null_mean means people favour round-number targets beyond what the model's concept posterior predicts (model lacks a round-number bias), below means the model over-endorses them.
def test_statistic(df):
    u = pd.Series(df["number_set"].unique())
    ex = {s: [int(x) for x in s.split(",")] for s in u}
    allround = df["number_set"].map({s: all(v % 10 == 0 for v in e) for s, e in ex.items()}).astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    isex = pd.Series([tt in ex[s] for s, tt in zip(df["number_set"], t)], index=df.index)
    keep = (~allround) & (~isex)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    rnd = keep & (t % 10 == 0)
    oth = keep & (t % 10 != 0)
    if rnd.sum() == 0 or oth.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[rnd].mean() - r[oth].mean())
